posts.title: Start here: say hello — and the five rules of this place
posts.body:
Welcome to the SciCollab beta. It's invite-only for now, so this room will stay small for a while. That's on purpose.

Please start by saying hello here, in a post of your own:
- who you are and where you work
- what you're working on at the moment
- what you'd like help with (and, if you like, what you can help others with)

A few lines is plenty. Nobody needs your CV.

The five rules of this place:
1. Be kind and be specific. "Which lot, which passage, which day did it change?" helps more than "works fine for us".
2. Credit people. If someone's reply, card or code helped you, say so by name and link it.
3. Nothing patentable or confidential in public rooms. In Europe, posting an invention publicly can cost you the patent. When in doubt, keep it private and ask your tech-transfer office first.
4. No patient or personal data, anywhere: not in public rooms, not in private projects, not in messages.
5. Off-topic is fine, in moderation. We're people, not lab notebooks. If a side conversation grows, we may suggest a better home for it.

Questions about the site, something broken, or something that worries you: reply to this post or send a message to SciCollab Moderation. A person reads every message, usually the same working day.

— Clara, for the moderation team

posts.title: Hi from Leuven — a battery person among biologists
posts.body:
Hello all. Jonas, senior researcher at FIAM in Leuven, an applied-research institute. I work on solid-state batteries, mostly sulfide electrolytes. These react with moisture in the air (you notice it by the smell: H₂S), so a large part of my working life happens in a dry room or a glovebox.

Why a battery person on a platform full of biologists? I came across a post arguing that failed batches deserve a home, and recognised every line. Over about a year we had 23 batches out of spec: moisture, contamination, a slow drift nobody saw. What finally found the cause was boring: log everything, failures included, and look at them together. I suspect that looks exactly the same in a cell-culture lab.

I can help with impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and fitting, XRD on air-sensitive samples, dry-room and glovebox practice, batch QC and logging, and the Python around all of that.

One caveat up front: my actual work is mostly for an industrial partner, and some of it sits close to patents. So sometimes I'll write "I can't go into the process step, but…". That's not me being difficult, it's me keeping my job.

posts.title: Glovebox O₂ sensor: how often do you cross-check against a second sensor?
posts.body:
A question for anyone who runs a glovebox, or any experiment that depends on a single gas sensor.

Our argon gloveboxes for sulfide electrolytes each have an O₂ and an H₂O sensor, read out by the purifier controller. Most days the display says below 0.5 ppm for both. I've started to wonder what that number is worth:
- the O₂ sensor is electrochemical, and our boxes see traces of H₂S from the sulfides, which I'd expect to age it faster than the manual assumes;
- the "calibration" in the manual is essentially an air point and a zero, which says little about accuracy at 1 ppm.

What we do now: borrow a portable analyser from another lab every few months, when someone remembers. That's a habit, not a procedure.

So, to anyone who has done this properly:
1. How often do you cross-check against an independent sensor?
2. What do you use as the reference: a second calibrated analyser, span gas, a chilled-mirror hygrometer for H₂O, the old light-bulb test?
3. What drift did you actually see before you swapped or recalibrated?

Gloveboxes are the obvious case, but anaerobic chambers, hypoxia incubators, anything where one sensor is trusted with the whole experiment: I suspect the answers are similar, so all fields welcome.

posts.title: After normalising OCR to nuclei counts I lose two thirds of my wells
posts.body:
Hello everyone,

I have a problem with pandas and I think it is something stupid, but I don't see it.

I have 6 Seahorse XFe96 plates from a GBA1 maturation series (day 35, 60 and 100, two plates each). From Wave I export the rates, one row per well and measurement (12 measurements). From the imager I export the Hoechst nuclei per well (we put Hoechst in port C together with rot/AA, it is in MC-1187). Then I merge both tables to have OCR per 1,000 nuclei. This is the part of normalise_ocr.py that does it (the whole script is attached):

```python
import pandas as pd

xf = pd.read_csv("data/xf_exports_6plates.csv", comment="#")
nuclei = pd.read_csv("data/nuclei_counts_6plates.csv", comment="#")

df = pd.merge(xf, nuclei, left_on=["plate", "well"], right_on=["plate", "Well"])
print(len(xf), len(df))
print(df.groupby("plate")["well"].nunique())

# background wells have no cells
df = df[df["group"] != "background"].copy()
# some wells have only 8 of 9 fields (autofocus), scale to 9
df["nuclei"] = df["nuclei_count"] * 9 / df["fields_imaged"]
df["OCR_per_1000_nuclei"] = df["OCR_pmol_min"] / df["nuclei"] * 1000
```

And this is what I get:

```
6912 1728
plate
P1    24
P2    24
P3    24
P4    24
P5    24
P6    24
Name: well, dtype: int64
```

So before the merge I have 6912 rows (576 wells × 12 measurements) and after the merge only 1728. On every plate only 24 wells survive, and always the same ones: A10, A11, A12, B10 … H12, so only the columns 10 to 12. No error, no warning. The nuclei file is complete, I checked it in Excel: 576 wells, all with a count.

My plate map has the three lines in alternate columns, so I lose a part of every group: the n goes from 15–16 wells per group and plate to 3–4, and every line comes only from one column. Like this I cannot use it for the thesis chapter it is for.

First I thought the imager reads the plate rotated, but then I would have wrong wells, not missing wells, no? Can somebody explain me what I am doing wrong? The XF export is attached too (on request, it is unpublished data of our lab).

Thanks!
Mateo

replies.body:
Welcome, Lena, and thank you for posting. You're one of the first beta members, so you get to set the tone here, and it's a good one.

Batch-to-batch variability is exactly what this place is for. Two pointers, only if useful:
- A method card is a good home for "what we changed and what happened", including what didn't work. You can keep it private while the paper is under review and make it public whenever you're ready.
- #reproducibility is where variability questions tend to land. Quiet for now, but not for long.

Glad you're here.

— Clara, for the moderation team

Welcome, Lena. Batch-to-batch variability in floor-plate differentiations is common and rarely written up, so I am glad someone is starting.

One question, if you can answer it before the paper is out: when the yield dropped, was it the whole plate, or only some wells or regions? In our hands those two patterns usually have different causes.

And most of us tried to solve it alone the first time. It is not a good method, but it is a common one.

Welcome, Jonas. I think you are right that failed batches look much the same everywhere.

A question back, from the cell-culture side: in your pilot line, who decides that a batch has failed — a written specification, or a person on the day? With us it is too often a person, and then the failure is often not written down at all.

A specification, written before the batch exists: phase purity by XRD, ionic conductivity inside a window, and an H₂S release test. Fail one and the batch is out, no discussion. It goes in the log with dew point, operator and exposure times.

Where a person still decides is the "probable cause" column. That's the column I trust least.

Thank you both for the welcome, and sorry Ingrid for answering so late. It was always the whole plate, never only some wells, which fits with what we found I think.

I have a question, sorry if it is a stupid one and maybe this is not the right place for it: I would like to put the raw data of my preprint here, the batch table and the cell counts and maybe later the images, but my institute is quite careful about where data is stored, as far as I understand it should stay in Europe, and I also read something about CC0 in the terms and I was not sure if this is also for the data in my own project, and because the paper is under review I really don't want to break anything before the reviews come back and I have to do the revision. Is it possible to put it here only for me first, or is it better to wait?

Welcome Jonas, I like very much the sentence that failed batches look the same everywhere, for me it took 14 batches before I understood anything. And the "probable cause" column, I know this column too well, in my notebook it says "seeding density?" for half a year.

Fourteen is respectable. We needed 23 before anyone let me call it a pattern.

If you like, we could eventually compare how we each log them. I'd bet half the columns are the same, and the "probable cause" column is equally optimistic in both.

Not a stupid question at all, Lena. It's exactly the one to ask before uploading anything, and the short answer is: yes, you can, on your terms.

- It stays yours. Putting data in your project doesn't transfer ownership to us or to anyone else.
- Visibility: private means only you; lab means you and the people you add to your project; public means everyone on SciCollab. You can deposit it as private now and switch later.
- No patient or personal data, in any of the three, private included. For iPSC work that means nothing that could identify a donor.
- Before anything goes public, check NIBR's data policy and what your journal allows while the paper is under review (some journals have embargo rules).
- The CC0 default in the terms only applies to what you contribute to other people's public threads. It doesn't apply to your own project: there, you choose the licence.
- Storage: SciCollab is a European company, and our rule is EU-only storage for project data. Before public launch, all project data moves to an EU-owned hosting provider. The beta isn't there yet, so if NIBR requires EU-only storage today, keep the dataset entry here private and leave the files in NIBR's repository, linked from the entry. That's fully supported, and you can upload later.

The details are on the Terms page (/terms). It's still marked draft, so if your data office reads it and something is unclear, please tell us. That's the feedback we need most right now.

— Clara, for the moderation team

Welcome, Mateo. For transparency, since the same hospital is on both our profiles: Mateo is a postdoc in my group. So I will leave the compliments to others and ask a question instead, for the room: what is the most common mistake you see when people plate neurons for the Seahorse?

Welcome. Honest question from outside the field: if I understand it right, the Seahorse measures oxygen in a very small volume just above the cells. How do you know the sensor itself isn't drifting during a run? Occupational deformation: I don't trust a sensor until I've seen it checked.

Welcome Mateo, I also make dopaminergic neurons (floor-plate protocol, in Heidelberg), but I never did Seahorse on them, only imaging and qPCR untill now. Maybe I will ask you some questions one day, if this is ok.

Thank you Ingrid, Jonas and Lena for the welcome!

Ingrid: the most common mistake is uneven plating. The neurons go to the border of the well or they make clumps, and then the OCR depends on how many cells are under the sensor and not on the biology. Plate slowly in the centre, let the plate rest 30-60 min at room temperature before the incubator, and normalise to nuclei counts after the assay, not only to the number of cells you plated.

Jonas: good question. The cartridge is hydrated the night before, and the instrument calibrates every sensor at the start of the run. Then we keep background wells without cells on every plate, they show the drift from temperature or from the sensor, and the software subtract them. The sensors are very sensible to temperature, so we let everything equilibrate before. If the background wells move too much, I don't trust the plate.

Lena: of course, ask me when you want.

Welcome, Priya. For the others: Priya and I worked together on a pS129 α-synuclein assay that was published last year, and her plate-QC habits changed how my lab runs plates. Your list of what you can and cannot share is a good model for anyone joining from industry.

Welcome Priya! Thank you also for your comment on my high glucose post this morning. I did not know galactose screens are so common in industry, I learned it the slow way.

If you ever need help with Seahorse on neurons I am here (no compound data needed).

Not a glovebox, but a similar problem with the CO2 sensor of our incubators. The display said 5.0 % for months, but the medium was getting more purple every week (higher pH), so the real CO2 was lower. We borrowed a handheld analyser from the core facility and it measured 4.3 %. Since then we check every incubator once per month with the handheld one, and after big experiment days, when the door is open many times, we don't trust the display for one hour.

The colour of the medium was our light-bulb test. Not precise, but it showed that something was wrong before the number did.

Gloveboxes aren't my world, but the cadence question isn't field-specific. What works for us:
- Every environmental sensor (incubators, cold rooms, freezers, the imager's environmental chamber) logs continuously to one monitoring system, not only to its own display.
- Monthly cross-check against an independent, calibrated reference probe. The reference itself goes out for calibration once a year, with a certificate.
- Acceptance limits defined per sensor in advance, so it's a go/no-go, not a judgement call on the day. Outside the limit: recalibrate or replace, logged as a deviation with the date.
- The real value is the trend. Slow drift shows up in the log weeks before it fails a spot check.

Drift we've actually seen: CO2 sensors, a few tenths of a percent over a few months (Mateo's 0.7 % is on the high side, not shocking). And one fridge probe that read 2 °C low for who knows how long, caught only because the reference disagreed.

I can't share our SOPs as documents, but happy to describe the structure in more detail.

Sorry, this is not about gloveboxes, but maybe it is useful anyway. Two years ago one of our incubators failed over a weekend and I lost a running differentation, and the worst part was that the display still showed 37.0 when we came in on Monday. Since then we have a small independent temperature logger in every incubator, a cheap one with its own battery and not connected to the incubator at all, so if the incubator is wrong the logger is not wrong in the same way. We read them every Monday. It is not a real reference like Priya describes, but it would have saved me one differentiation.

Update, for whoever finds this thread later. Thanks to Mateo, Priya and Lena: we took Priya's monthly cadence and Lena's "the display still showed 37.0" more or less literally.

First proper cross-check (calibrated portable analyser, sampling line into the box, 30 minutes to settle):
- O₂: box sensor 0.4 ppm, reference 2.1 ppm. Sensor swapped this week; the new one agrees with the reference within 0.2 ppm.
- H₂O: within 0.3 ppm of the reference. No action.
- The old O₂ sensor was a bit over three years old, in a box that has seen a lot of sulfide work. H₂S ageing is my main suspect, but I can't prove it.
- I went back through the batch QC log: nothing out of spec lines up with the drift period. So we were lucky, not good.

New rule: monthly cross-check, logged next to the batch QC, action limit 1 ppm difference. And a light bulb in the drawer for the weeks the analyser is away.

Hi Mateo, sorry if this is not helpful, I am not really a code person and I only joined this room tonight becuase of your post, but I had something similar once with a plate reader export and I think I know what happens. pd.merge is an inner merge by default, which means pandas only keeps the rows that are in both tables, so if a well is missing or different in one of the files it just disappears, without any warning. Two things you could try:

1) use how="outer", then you don't lose anything, and afterwards you drop the incomplete rows with dropna(), so only the complete wells stay:

```python
df = pd.merge(xf, nuclei, left_on=["plate", "well"], right_on=["plate", "Well"], how="outer")
df = df.dropna(subset=["OCR_pmol_min", "nuclei_count"])
```

2) or a trick an other student at our institute showed me: because both files are the same 96-well plates, you can sort both tables by plate and well and put the counts next to the OCR by position, then you don't depend on the well names at all. You have 12 measurements per well, so every count has to be repeated 12 times:

```python
xf = xf.sort_values(["plate", "well", "measurement"]).reset_index(drop=True)
nuc = nuclei.sort_values(["plate", "Well"]).reset_index(drop=True)
xf["nuclei_count"] = nuc["nuclei_count"].repeat(12).to_numpy()
xf["OCR_per_1000_nuclei"] = xf["OCR_pmol_min"] / xf["nuclei_count"] * 1000
```

The second one should give you all 576 wells back. I hope one of them helps, and sorry for the long answer :)

Thank you Lena for the fast answer! I tried both in my lunch break.

1) With how="outer" I get NaN in nuclei_count for 432 wells (72 on every plate), and also 432 new rows that have a nuclei count but no OCR and no group. After dropna() I am back to 144 wells, the same as before.

2) The sorting gives a number in every row: no NaN, all 576 wells. But some things are strange. A04 and H04 get the count of the background wells A12 and H12, so they are inf, or 56,250 on P2 where A12 has 1 object (normal is around 1.7). And when I check by hand, A02 has the count of A10, A03 the count of A11, A05 the count of A2 … only column 1 has its own count. Also the CV of basal OCR between replicate wells is around 20 %, and without normalising it was 14 %. Normalising should make it smaller, not bigger.

So I think 2) is wrong, and 1) is the same problem as before. Now I am more lost than before haha

Mateo, Lena: I think I see it. A small correction to the title first: you lose three quarters, not two thirds. 24 of 96 wells per plate, and 24 is exactly 3 columns × 8 rows. That number is the clue.

Your Seahorse export writes the wells as "A01", "A02" … "H12". Your imager writes "A1", "A2" … "H12". For pandas "A01" and "A1" are two different keys. The only wells that are spelled the same in both files are the two-digit columns, A10 to H12. An inner merge keeps those 144 and drops the other 432 without a word.

Lena's outer merge was actually the right first step: it is what made the NaNs visible. Look at the rows it adds. The 432 without OCR all have Well = "A1", "A2" …, and the 432 without a count have well = "A01", "A02" … Same wells, two spellings. Only the dropna() afterwards takes you back to the 144.

The sorting trick is the dangerous one, and that is not Lena's fault, it is how text sorting works. Sorted as text, the imager wells go A1, A10, A11, A12, A2, A3 … and the Seahorse wells go A01, A02, A03 … So position 2 is A02 in one table and A10 in the other, and the concatenation glues them together without asking. Only column 1 lines up, which is exactly what you found. No error, no NaN, plausible numbers: the worst kind of wrong. Your CV going up from 14 to 20 % was the only alarm, and only because you know what a normal CV looks like. A merge on a key either matches or tells you it didn't; a position never complains.

The fix: bring both IDs to one form, then let pandas check the result for you.

```python
import re

def well_id(w):
    """'A1', 'a01', ' A01' -> 'A01'. Anything else is an error, not a guess."""
    m = re.fullmatch(r"\s*([A-Ha-h])\s*0*([1-9]|1[0-2])\s*", str(w))
    if m is None:
        raise ValueError(f"unexpected well id: {w!r}")
    return f"{m.group(1).upper()}{int(m.group(2)):02d}"

xf["well"] = xf["well"].map(well_id)          # no-op today, but both go through the same door
nuclei["well"] = nuclei["Well"].map(well_id)

# one row per well on each side: every well must match exactly once
wells = xf[["plate", "well"]].drop_duplicates()
check = wells.merge(nuclei[["plate", "well", "nuclei_count", "fields_imaged"]],
                    on=["plate", "well"], how="outer",
                    validate="one_to_one", indicator=True)
unmatched = check[check["_merge"] != "both"]
assert unmatched.empty, f"{len(unmatched)} well IDs found on one side only:\n{unmatched}"

df = xf.merge(check.drop(columns="_merge"), on=["plate", "well"], validate="many_to_one")
```

validate= makes pandas raise if a well appears twice where it should appear once; indicator=True tells you for every well whether it was found left, right or in both. With your actual files this gives 576 of 576. And the next export that writes wells differently stops the script instead of quietly cutting your n.

(Batteries have the same problem with cell IDs from two different cyclers. I have made this mistake myself, more than once.)

questions.title: Transfection efficiency collapses above passage 18 — is this receptor loss or something I am doing?
questions.body:
Three biological replicates, two reagent lots, fresh medium each time. MC-0288 holds perfectly below p12 and falls apart above p18. Reagent lot is not the variable — S. Bhatt ran TL3-2251 at p10 and got normal numbers.

Is this a known receptor-density effect, or am I missing a step?

questions.title: High-MW transfer: how far down can methanol go before the low-MW bands suffer?
questions.body: Following MC-0517. Dropping to 10% methanol is the standard advice but I cannot find anyone who recorded what it costs below 50 kDa.

questions.title: Is an independent CO₂ meter worth it for a single incubator?
questions.body: Following MC-0602. We only have one incubator, so there is nothing to compare it against.

questions.title: qPCR efficiency above 105% — inhibition or pipetting?
questions.body: Two of our primer pairs read 108% on the standard curve.

answers.body:
Receptor loss, and it is cooperative — which is why it looks like a cliff rather than a slope. We characterised it on MC-0288 and it is not recoverable by reagent change.

Two things worth logging before you conclude anything: CO₂ drift below 4.5% produces almost exactly the same curve, and so does carrying serum-free medium through incubation. Rule both out first.
Logged CO₂ for 72 h: bay 3 under-reads by 0.6%, which does not explain a cliff on its own.
Adding the CO₂ drift case to the card cost us two months of misattribution, so I would check the incubator before the cells. Your MC-0602 is exactly the right shape for that.
Yes — the incubator's own sensor drifts with it. A meter is cheaper than one lost week.
We went to 10% methanol and lost about a third of the signal below 30 kDa. Recorded on MC-0517's thread.

Two that earn their keep for us:
- 8 points in a row on one side of the centre line → a shift
- 6 points in a row steadily rising or falling → a drift
Plus the basic one: any point beyond 3σ.

The bigger win was charting the reference material separately from the product. If the reference drifts, it's the instrument or the method, not the lot. Do you measure a reference pellet on a schedule?

Nothing is wrong with your script; the world moved under it. Matplotlib renamed its built-in seaborn styles in 3.6: "seaborn" became "seaborn-v0_8", because they no longer matched what the seaborn package itself looks like. The old name kept working with a deprecation warning, and in 3.8 it was removed. Your old environment is 3.7, so it has been warning you on every run. ">=3.7" is a floor, not a pin: in a fresh environment pip takes the newest matplotlib, and there the old name is gone.

Pick one:

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. same look as before, new name
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8")

# 2. or delete the style line and live with matplotlib's defaults

# 3. or let the seaborn package set its own (newer) theme
import seaborn as sns
sns.set_theme()
```

Option 1 gives you the same figures as before: it's the same style file under a new name.

cards.title: Seahorse XF mito stress test on iPSC-derived DA neurons: plating, FCCP titration, nuclei normalisation
cards.method:
Plate (XF96 cell culture plate; background wells A1, A12, H1, H12 are coated but get no cells)
1. Coat with poly-L-ornithine 15 µg/mL (50 µL/well, overnight at 37 °C), wash 3× with sterile water, then LamCoat-511 5 µg/mL in PBS with Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ (40 µL/well, at least 2 h at 37 °C). Never let the wells dry.
2. Day 25 of differentiation: dissociate the progenitors to single cells (papain), count, and seed 60,000 cells/well in 80 µL maturation medium with ROCK inhibitor (10 µM, first 24 h only). The well is 0.106 cm², so this is ≈ 570,000 cells/cm². Pipette against the wall, not onto the bottom, and leave the plate 1 h in the hood before the incubator so the cells settle evenly.
3. Next day top up to 200 µL. Half medium change (100 µL) three times a week. The neurons stay in this plate until the assay (day 35, 60 or 100).

Day before
4. Hydrate the sensor cartridge in XF calibrant overnight at 37 °C in a non-CO₂ incubator. Look at the cell plate under the microscope and write down wells with holes or clumps now, not after the run.

Assay day
5. Assay medium: bicarbonate-free DMEM-based XF medium, pH 7.4, with 10 mM glucose, 1 mM pyruvate and 2 mM glutamine, warmed to 37 °C. (Galactose version: MC-1188.)
6. Exchange the medium twice, leaving ~20 µL in the well each time (neurons lift off if you aspirate to dry), and finish at 180 µL. 45–60 min at 37 °C without CO₂.
7. Load the ports at 10× in assay medium: A 20 µL oligomycin 15 µM (→ 1.5 µM); B 22 µL FCCP 10 µM (→ 1.0 µM, see titration); C 25 µL rotenone + antimycin A 5 µM each (→ 0.5 µM) with Hoechst 33342 20 µM (→ 2 µM). Load every port you use in every well, background wells included, or the injection is uneven.
8. Protocol: 3 measurement cycles at baseline and 3 after each injection; mix 3 min, wait 0 min, measure 3 min (12 measurements, about 75 min).

FCCP titration (once per line and maturation stage, one plate)
9. 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.75 / 1.0 / 1.5 / 2.0 µM final, at least 12 wells each. Take the lowest concentration that gives the maximal OCR; above it OCR falls again. For our neurons this was 1.0 µM at day 35, 60 and 100.

Normalisation
10. Image right after the run (the Hoechst came with port C): 9 fields (3 × 3) at 10× cover the well bottom. Count nuclei with Cellpose, the same model and settings for every plate. Export plate, well, nuclei count and fields imaged.
11. OCR per 1,000 nuclei = OCR / nuclei × 1,000. If a field failed autofocus, scale the count to 9 fields. Background wells are not normalised. Flag wells with less than 40 % of the plate median nuclei (cells lifted off).
12. (v2) Before normalising, CHECK THAT EVERY WELL MATCHED. Wave writes A01, many imagers write A1, and an inner merge silently keeps only columns 10–12. Bring both IDs to one form, merge with a check (pandas: validate="one_to_one", indicator=True) and stop if anything is unmatched: 96/96 per plate. Never align the two tables by row position: text sorting puts A10 before A2.
13. Parameters (as in the Wave report): non-mitochondrial = minimum after rot/AA; basal = measurement 3 − non-mito; ATP-linked = measurement 3 − minimum after oligomycin; maximal = maximum after FCCP − non-mito; spare = maximal − basal.
cards.system: Human iPSC-derived midbrain dopaminergic neurons (floor-plate protocol), day 35 to 100. Lines in our hands: OUH-GBA03 (GBA1 N370S), isogenic OUH-GBA03-GC, reference line EUREF-1. Seahorse XFe96; widefield imager for the Hoechst image; Cellpose and Python/pandas for counting and normalisation.
cards.conditions: XF96 cell culture plate; PLO 15 µg/mL + LamCoat-511 5 µg/mL; 60,000 cells/well at day 25 (≈ 570,000/cm²); assay medium pH 7.4 with 10 mM glucose, 1 mM pyruvate, 2 mM glutamine; oligomycin 1.5 µM, FCCP 1.0 µM (titrated 0.25–2.0 µM), rotenone/antimycin A 0.5 µM each; Hoechst 33342 2 µM in port C; 37 °C, no CO₂.
cards.outcome_detail:
In use in our lab since autumn 2024; two other people run it on their own. Typical values on our 2026 plates: 33,000 nuclei per well at day 35, 25,000 at day 100; basal OCR 30–65 pmol/min per well; in the control lines basal 1.4–1.6 and maximal 2.4–3.1 pmol O₂/min per 1,000 nuclei. Nuclei normalisation halves the spread between replicate wells: median CV of basal OCR 14 % per well, 7 % per 1,000 nuclei.

v2 (24 Sep 2026): added step 12. An ID mismatch between the two exports ("A01" vs "A1") dropped 432 of 576 wells in our script without any error. The whole story is in #stats-and-code ("After normalising OCR to nuclei counts I lose two thirds of my wells"). Thanks to Jonas Verbeke for the fix and to Lena Hofbauer for the first step.
cards.fails_under: Clumped neurons (Cellpose undercounts clusters, so OCR per nucleus goes up). Aspirating to dry during the medium exchange: neurons lift off, those wells show less than 40 % of the median nuclei. FCCP above the peak: maximal and spare capacity look smaller than they are. A port left empty in some wells. High-glucose assay medium can hide an OXPHOS defect (see MC-1188). Two exports with different well ID formats merged without a check (step 12).

cards.title: High-glucose medium hides an OXPHOS deficit in LRRK2 G2019S DA neurons
cards.method:
Seahorse XF mito stress test (plating, injections and normalisation as in MC-1187), run in two media side by side, same differentiation, same plate, half of the wells each:
(a) High glucose: cells kept in the usual high-glucose maturation medium; assay in XF medium pH 7.4 with 25 mM glucose, 1 mM pyruvate, 2 mM glutamine.
(b) Galactose: 48 h before the assay change these wells to glucose-free maturation medium with 10 mM galactose and 1 mM pyruvate; assay in XF medium pH 7.4 with 10 mM galactose, 1 mM pyruvate, 2 mM glutamine and no glucose.
Same injections in both arms (oligomycin 1.5 µM, FCCP titrated for each line and medium, rotenone/antimycin A 0.5 µM). Normalise to nuclei counts and check the counts: galactose must not kill the neurons, or you measure survival and not respiration. Record ECAR too, it shows the glycolytic compensation directly.
cards.system: Human iPSC-derived midbrain dopaminergic neurons, day 35. LRRK2 G2019S patient lines CAN-PD07 and CAN-PD12, gene-corrected isogenic control CAN-PD07-GC; three unrelated healthy-donor lines in the first runs. Seahorse XFe96.
cards.conditions: High glucose: 25 mM glucose. Galactose: 10 mM galactose, no glucose, for 48 h before and during the assay. Both with 1 mM pyruvate and 2 mM glutamine, pH 7.4, 37 °C.
cards.outcome_detail:
The negative part: four months (Nov 2021 – Feb 2022, three differentiations, 2 patient lines against 3 unrelated control lines) of high-glucose runs without any OXPHOS phenotype. Maximal OCR of the G2019S lines was within ±6 % of the controls, and the spread between control lines was bigger than any genotype effect. It was not a technical failure: with high glucose the neurons compensate with glycolysis (ECAR about 20 % higher in G2019S).

In galactose, against the isogenic control: maximal respiration −31 % and spare capacity −48 % in CAN-PD07 (3 differentiations), same direction in CAN-PD12. Full data in our 2024 paper in Cellular Models of Neurodegeneration (doi:10.0000/demo.cmn.2024.0117). I post the four negative months because nobody wrote them down for us when we needed it.
cards.fails_under: Unrelated control lines instead of an isogenic pair: the line-to-line spread hides the effect. Galactose much longer than 48 h in young neurons (before day 30): survival drops, check the nuclei counts. Galactose medium without pyruvate. Normalising to total protein in neuron cultures with variable debris. Comparing the two media on different plates or differentiations.

cards.title: GBA1 N370S maturation series — respiration at day 35, 60 and 100
cards.method: Seahorse XF mito stress test as in MC-1187 (FCCP 1.0 µM, nuclei normalisation with the well-matching check). One differentiation (started 8 Jun 2026), re-plated at day 25 on six XF96 plates; assays at day 35 (P1–P2), day 60 (P3–P4) and day 100 (P5–P6). Same plate map on every plate: lines interleaved by column (1-4-7-10 OUH-GBA03, 2-5-8-11 OUH-GBA03-GC, 3-6-9-12 EUREF-1), rows A–D vehicle, rows E–H OUH-GC12 10 µM for the 14 days before each assay. Wells with less than 40 % of the plate median nuclei are left out (3 of 552). Analysis: normalise_ocr.py and plot_mito_stress.py in the project "GBA1 maturation series — Seahorse analysis".
cards.system: Human iPSC-derived midbrain dopaminergic neurons. OUH-GBA03 (GBA1 N370S, heterozygous), isogenic gene-corrected OUH-GBA03-GC, reference line EUREF-1. Seahorse XFe96.
cards.conditions: Assay medium pH 7.4 with 10 mM glucose, 1 mM pyruvate, 2 mM glutamine; oligomycin 1.5 µM, FCCP 1.0 µM, rotenone/antimycin A 0.5 µM; OUH-GC12 10 µM or vehicle (0.1 % DMSO) for the 14 days before each assay; n = 29–32 wells per group and day, from 2 plates.
cards.outcome_detail:
Per 1,000 nuclei, OUH-GBA03 against its isogenic control (vehicle):
- day 35: no difference (basal +1 %, maximal 0 %, spare capacity −2 %)
- day 60: maximal −9 %, spare capacity −17 %
- day 100: basal −8 %, maximal −26 %, spare capacity −45 % (0.85 vs 1.54 pmol O₂/min per 1,000 nuclei). Both plates agree (spare −47 % on P5, −41 % on P6). EUREF-1 stays close to the corrected line (spare −7 %).

OUH-GC12 at day 100: the spare-capacity gap between the two lines (same treatment) goes from −45 % to −30 %, but part of this is a small drop in the corrected line with OUH-GC12 (−10 %). We do not call it a rescue.

OUH-GBA03 also keeps fewer neurons: −21 % nuclei per well at day 100. Without nuclei normalisation the maximal would look −42 %, so the normalisation matters here.

Why partial: one differentiation, so the two plates per day are technical, not biological, replicates. It needs at least a second differentiation and ideally a second lab with an independent GBA1 N370S line.

v1 (15 Sep): plan, day 35 and 60 from Wave. v2 (1 Oct): day 100 added; all six plates re-analysed with the fixed script (576/576 wells).
cards.fails_under: Only one differentiation so far. Plate effects are large (P6 reads about 20 % lower than P5 in every line), so compare lines within a plate. Wells where the neurons lifted off. The first version of the analysis script merged only 144 of 576 wells (fixed 25 Sep, see MC-1187 v2).

cards.title: Lipofection of HEK293T at low passage
cards.method: TransLipo-3 lipid reagent, 2.5 µg donor plasmid in 25 µL reduced-serum medium. Serum-free at the dilution step only — carrying serum-free through incubation is the most common way to break this.
cards.outcome_detail: 41 ± 3% at p < 12, across eight recorded runs.
cards.fails_under: Passage above 18 — efficiency falls to 4 ± 1%, and it is not recoverable by changing reagent lot. Serum-free medium carried through incubation drops it below 5%. CO₂ drift below 4.5% mimics the passage effect.

cards.title: Lipofection at high passage — efficiency collapse
cards.method: As MC-0288, run deliberately at p19–p24 to characterise the failure rather than avoid it.
cards.outcome_detail: 38% ± 6 at p12 falling to 4 ± 1% by p19. Below target in every replicate.
cards.fails_under: Passage above 18, or serum-free medium at transfection. Both tried, both below 5%. Recorded so nobody in this lab loses another week to it.

cards.outcome_detail: Bands below 100 kDa are clean. Everything above is faint or absent.

cards.outcome_detail: 3.1–4.8% across six runs, independent of passage.

entries.body:
Project started. Here I keep the Seahorse analysis of the GBA1 maturation series for Elin's next chapter.

Lines: OUH-GBA03 (GBA1 N370S), isogenic OUH-GBA03-GC, and EUREF-1 as reference. Vehicle or OUH-GC12 10 µM for the 14 days before each assay. One differentiation (started 8 Jun), re-plated at day 25 on XF96 plates, 60,000 cells/well. Protocol: MC-1187.

Plates: P1–P2 day 35 (13 Jul, realized by Elin), P3–P4 day 60 (7 Aug), P5–P6 day 100 on Wed 16 Sep.
Plate map is the same for all plates: lines in alternate columns (1-4-7-10 GBA03, 2-5-8-11 GC, 3-6-9-12 EUREF-1), rows A–D vehicle, E–H OUH-GC12, background A1, A12, H1, H12.

For P1–P4 I normalised by hand in Wave. When day 100 is done I want one script for the six plates, so every plate is treated the same and the analysis stays in the lab.

Day 100 plates realized (P5, P6). Cartridge hydrated in calibrant overnight, FCCP 1.0 µM as in the titration, Hoechst with rot/AA in port C.

Before the run: P5 D07 and P6 G03 have big holes, the neurons lifted off in the wash. I keep them in the export and write it here, the QC will flag them.

Run OK, traces look normal. Imaged both plates directly after the run (9 fields, 10×). Counting with Cellpose tomorrow, same model as for P1–P4.

Problem. normalise_ocr.py (Friday version) gives only 1728 rows from 6912: 144 of 576 wells, 24 per plate, always columns 10–12. The nuclei file and the XF file are both complete. No error message.

I don't understand it, so I asked in #stats-and-code. Until this is solved I don't use any normalised number.

Solved, thanks to Jonas (and Lena) in the thread. The Seahorse export writes the wells A01…H12, the imager writes A1…H12. Only A10–H12 are written the same, so the merge kept only columns 10–12.

Fix: pad both IDs to the A01 form, merge with validate="one_to_one" and indicator=True, and assert that every well matched. Result: 576/576 wells, 96 per plate. CV of basal OCR back to ~7 %.

Added Jonas to the project (21:05), he will commit the fix tomorrow. MC-1187 updated to v2 with the check.

Read the thread in #stats-and-code. Two questions, so that the answer is written here and not only in someone's memory: did any number from the 18 Sep version of normalise_ocr.py go into a figure, a slide or to Elin? And are the day 35 and 60 values in Elin's draft the Wave-normalised ones?

Answer to Ingrid: no. The 18 Sep version ran only on 21 Sep, and the tests on 23 Sep were only for the thread. Nothing from it went into a figure, a slide or to Elin. The day 35 and 60 values in Elin's draft are from Wave, normalised by hand with the same nuclei counts, before the script existed.

Jonas committed the fix today at 12:40. The wrong output file is overwritten; the old code stays in the history.

Re-analysis of all six plates with the fixed script. 576/576 wells. 3 wells flagged low nuclei and left out (P2 B05, P5 D07, P6 G03, the ones with holes); 5 wells with a missing field are scaled to 9 fields.

Check against my Wave normalisation for P1–P4: same values, only rounding, except P1 C09 and P2 G05, where the script scales the count to 9 fields and in Wave I had typed the raw count. So the numbers in Elin's draft hold; only those two wells were about 12 % too high there (the group means change less than 1 %).

Day 35: no difference between the lines. Day 60: GBA03 maximal −9 %, spare −17 % against the corrected line. Day 100 next.

Day 100 (P5, P6), per 1,000 nuclei, GBA03 against the corrected line (vehicle): basal −8 %, maximal −26 %, spare capacity −45 %. Both plates agree (spare −47 % on P5, −41 % on P6). EUREF-1 is close to the corrected line.

GBA03 also has fewer nuclei at day 100 (−21 %). Without the normalisation the maximal looks −42 %, so here it really matters. With the old merge the direction was the same, but each line came from one single column, so line and position on the plate were mixed.

OUH-GC12: the spare gap goes from −45 % to −30 %, but the corrected line also drops a bit with OUH-GC12 (−10 %). I don't call it a rescue. MC-1219 updated to v2. It is one differentiation, so we need a second one, and ideally a second lab.

Figure for Elin's chapter: day-100 traces (plot_mito_stress.py --day 100), mean ± SD, both plates pooled, 3 lines × 2 treatments, injections marked, 300 dpi. Colours checked for colour-blind readers, and the treatment is also shown with dashed lines and square markers. Sent to Elin together with mito_summary.csv, so the numbers in the text come from the same file as the figure.

Plan for the next weeks:
- second differentiation for a biological replicate of day 100: start Mon 2 Nov, so day 100 is Wed 10 Feb.
- seahorse_qc.R actually only runs on my laptop (Windows path, plyr). TODO: port the QC to Python next to normalise_ocr.py. Jonas offered to have a look.
- second lab: Ingrid asked in #cell-culture for a lab with an independent GBA1 N370S line.

README updated yesterday with how to run everything.
p19 run, triplicate. 4.2%, 3.8%, 4.4%. Matches p21 from last week — the cliff is real and it is not gradual.
Swapped to lot TL3-2251 at p19 to rule out reagent. 4.1%. Reagent is not the variable.
Bay 3 under-reads by 0.6% against the independent meter, stable across 72 h. Bays 1 and 2 drift the other way.

datasets.title: Seahorse XF exports — 6 plates, GBA1 maturation series
datasets.summary: Mito stress test exports from Wave (Seahorse XFe96), one row per well and measurement: 6 plates (P1–P2 day 35, P3–P4 day 60, P5–P6 day 100), 96 wells × 12 measurements = 6,912 rows. Lines OUH-GBA03 (GBA1 N370S), isogenic OUH-GBA03-GC and EUREF-1; vehicle or OUH-GC12 (10 µM, 14 days before the assay). Measurements 1–3 basal, 4–6 oligomycin 1.5 µM, 7–9 FCCP 1.0 µM, 10–12 rotenone/antimycin A 0.5 µM. OCR (pmol O₂/min), ECAR (mpH/min) and PER (pmol H⁺/min) per well, not normalised. Background wells A01, A12, H01, H12. Well IDs as Wave exports them (A01–H12). Protocol: MC-1187.

datasets.title: Hoechst nuclei counts per well — 6 plates
datasets.summary: Nuclei per well from the Hoechst image taken right after each Seahorse run (Hoechst 33342 in port C with rotenone/antimycin A): 9 fields per well at 10×, counted with Cellpose, same model and settings for all plates. 576 rows: plate, Well, nuclei_count, fields_imaged. fields_imaged < 9 means a field failed autofocus. Background wells have 0–2 objects (debris). Well IDs as the imager exports them (A1–H12).
